newsitem.title: UK: British shares gripped by rate anxieties.
newsitem.headline: British shares gripped by rate anxieties.

text.p: British stocks are likely to be in for another rocky ride next week but market watchers say that this week's share price falls may already have factored in mounting expectations for an imminent rise in U.S. interest rates.

After tumbling 74 points on Thursday, its biggest one-day loss since last December, the FTSE 100 index on Friday closed down for the fifth straight day when it ended the week at 4254.8, down 3.3 points on the day.
Market nerves are likely to continue until Tuesday's meeting of the U.S. Fed's policy-setting open market committee which may agree to an interest rate hike.
The London market is also likely to be kept on edge ahead of the May 1 election and the possibility of an increase in British interest rates.
"The market has displayed anxiety this week and there is no reason to think that anxiety is going to disappear soon," said Richard Jeffrey, stock market strategist at Charterhouse Tilney.
"The things it is anxious about, UK politics and UK interest rates, are not going to be resolved overnight."
After posting a record high as recently as last week, the UK's FTSE 100 index was likely to continue its recent decline as the first quarter of the year draws to a close, analysts said.
Fund managers take a quarterly look at their investment priorities, they noted.
But a sharp drop may not be on the cards.
"We have seen the panic stage and now we are more likely to go into a dull drift rather than a meltdown," said Ian Williams, strategist at Panmure Gordon.
"I think we are going down and 4,200 is quite likely and if we get there it will be a good buying opportunity on a 12-month view."

U.S. Treasury bonds, which set a benchmark for markets around the world, even managed to rally on Friday with the yield on the benchmark 30-year issue bouncing back after briefly rising through seven percent.

It was Alan Greenspan, chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve and arguably the most influential figure in world markets, who sent markets into a spin on Thursday with comments taken as a signal of a rate rise next week.
A Reuters poll of economists found that 34 out of 48 expect a rise of at least a quarter point in the Fed's short-term funds rate to 5.50 percent.
Yet what market experts are less sure of is how much further rates will rise from there.

Optimists believe a relatively small tightening in policy could be enough to pre-empt an inflationary burst of growth and keep on track the steady growth, low inflation scenario which has nurtured world markets for the past two years.
Yet Greenspan himself said the main effect of a rate rise now may not be felt until later this year and in 1998.
"If the next inflation figures look a bit strong people will probably say he wasn't pre-emptive," said Jeffrey of Charterhouse Tilney.
In the UK next week's main economic release is GDP for the fourth quarter of 1996, which is not expected to have a major impact on expectations of a rate rise here.
But with the ruling Conservatives trailing in opinion polls, UK markets remain concerned about the prospect of a post-election rate hike by the first Labour government in 18 years.
Labour's prospective finance minister Gordon Brown is also likely to want to show his financial credibility early on.
"The greater risk is that Brown overreacts," said Jeffrey at Charterhouse Tilney, who expects rates to be tightened progressively through the second half of 1997.
"Against the backdrop of a booming high street, a one percent base rate increase is likely to appear too tentative."
UK companies reporting next week include retailer Next Plc and lubricants group Burmah Castrol Plc.
